interactive.title: Drag the graph
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on sliding a graph. A graph sits on axes with the input along the bottom and the output up the side, and you grab it and drag it. A faint copy stays where it started, so you can see how far it has gone. The rule above the graph rewrites as you drag: f(x) + 2 for a slide up 2, f(x − 3) for a slide 3 to the right. One marked point on the graph shows its old and new coordinates side by side. A small three-row table underneath shows three inputs and their outputs, and as you drag it rewrites to show which inputs now give the old outputs. Slides snap to whole squares so points land on grid lines. Sliding up 2 adds 2 to every output, so the table keeps its inputs and each output grows by 2: the square y = x² takes the point (2, 4) to (2, 6). Sliding right 3 gives (x − 3)², which takes 3 off each input before squaring, so an input must be 3 bigger to give the old output: 3, 4 and 5 now give 0, 1 and 4, which 0, 1 and 2 gave before, and (2, 4) moves to (5, 4). Sliding left 2 gives (x + 2)², where −2, −1 and 0 give 0, 1 and 4. The graphs are the square, the cube y = x³ and the square root y = √x from lesson 3, and the 4 to 20 mA transmitter line from lesson 2, S(p) = 0.16p + 4, drawn with the line 0.16p beneath it as the faint copy, so the shift is its 4 mA. The square root is drawn from 0 to 9 and slides with its filled starting dot, so √(x − 4) starts at 4. Before each sideways slide a screen asks you to predict left or right, and then you drag to see. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, or two on a predict screen, and a wrong pick shows the slip that makes it, such as moving the wrong way or moving the input instead of the output.
interactive.ignores: Each graph shows only part of its curve, which carries on past the edge of the picture. The slides of 1, 2, 3 and 4, the 50% level and the 1 mA error are example values, kept to whole numbers so points land on grid lines; a graph can slide by any amount, a fraction too, and the rules still hold. The transmitter is drawn as its plain straight-line rule. Only ordinary (real) numbers are used.

explain.text:
Shifting a graph slides it without changing its shape. Add a number to the output and the graph slides up or down; add or take a number from the input inside the bracket and it slides left or right. The sideways move is the one that catches people out, and the function machine from lesson 1 shows why it goes the way it does.

f(x) + 2 means put x through the machine, then add 2 to what comes out. Take the square from lesson 3, f(x) = x². At x = 2 it gives 4, so x² + 2 gives 6. The input is the same and only its output is 2 higher, and that is true at every input, so every point rises 2 and the whole graph slides up 2. That is a [[vertical shift]], a slide straight up or down,[^1] and x² − 3 slides down 3 in the same way. You have met one before. The transmitter's rule from lesson 2, S(p) = 0.16p + 4, is a straight-line rule of the kind instruments use,[^2] and it is the line 0.16p lifted by its 4 mA, so the 8 mA that line gives at 50% becomes 12 mA. Sliding up changes no steepness, so the slope is still 0.16 mA per percent.

f(x − 3) means take 3 off the input first, then put what is left through the machine. So (x − 3)² gives 0 only when x − 3 is 0, which is at x = 3, not at 0. To get the old output 1 you now feed in 4, not 1, and to get 4 you feed in 5, not 2. Each input must be 3 bigger to give the old output, so every point sits 3 further right, and the graph slides 3 to the right. That is a [[horizontal shift]], a slide along the x-axis.[^3] In the same way f(x + 2) adds 2 before the machine, so each input can be 2 smaller, and the graph slides 2 to the left. A common slip is to move f(x + 3) to the right because the 3 is positive.[^4] One point settles it: find the input that makes the bracket 0. Everything about the graph slides with it, including where the machine starts: √x starts at 0, so √(x − 4) starts at 4. The two moves do not get in each other's way, so (x − 3)² + 2 slides right 3 and up 2, and its bottom moves from (0, 0) to (3, 2).

**Adding outside the bracket, f(x) + 3, slides the graph up 3;[^1] taking 3 off the input inside, f(x − 3), slides it 3 to the right, because each input must be 3 bigger to give the old output.**

analogy.text: Think of two identical heating timers, the second set 2 hours behind the first. Whatever the first does at 7 o'clock, the second does at 9, so its on-off chart is the first one's slid 2 hours to the right. To find what the late one does at 9, you ask what the early one did at 9 − 2 = 7: late(t) = early(t − 2), a minus inside that moves the chart right.
analogy.breaks: A day wraps round, so a timer's chart slid past midnight comes back in at the start of the day, while a function's graph just carries on sliding. A timer also copies only the sideways move: a slide up changes the outputs themselves, which no timer setting does.

practice.text:
- Up or down: look for a number added outside the bracket. f(x) + 3 slides the graph up 3, and f(x) − 3 slides it down 3.
- Left or right: look inside the bracket and find the input that makes it 0. The point that sat at input 0 now sits there. f(x − 3) slides right 3, and f(x + 3) slides left 3.
- Move one easy point, such as the bottom of a U, then the others: every point moves the same way by the same amount.
- Check one moved point in the new rule.

**Rule of thumb:** A number added outside the bracket moves it up or down, the way the sign says. For one inside, find the input that makes the bracket 0: the point that sat at input 0 now sits there.

**Worked example:** Sketch y = (x − 3)² + 2 from y = x². Inside, x − 3 is 0 at x = 3, so the graph slides 3 to the right. Outside, the + 2 slides it up 2. The bottom (0, 0) moves to (3, 2), and the points (1, 1) and (2, 4) move to (4, 3) and (5, 6). Check one: at x = 5, (5 − 3)² + 2 = 4 + 2 = 6.

**Common mistakes**
- Moving f(x + 3) to the right because the 3 is positive.[^4] The bracket is 0 at x = −3, so the graph moves left.
- Mixing up outside and inside. x² − 3 drops the graph 3; (x − 3)² slides it 3 to the right.
- Forgetting that where the machine starts slides too. √(x − 4) starts at x = 4, not 0.

checks.label: Adding or subtracting a constant k to a function shifts its graph up or down vertically by k units: on the first screen x² + 2 keeps every input and adds 2 to its output, so (2, 4) goes to (2, 6) and the table's 0, 1 and 4 become 2, 3 and 6; dragged to any whole square k, every point sits k higher at the same input

Adding or subtracting a constant to the x term shifts the graph left or right along the x-axis: (x − 3)² gives 0, 1 and 4 at inputs 3, 4 and 5, as x² did at 0, 1 and 2, so (2, 4) goes to (5, 4); (x + 2)² gives them at −2, −1 and 0; dragged sideways to any whole square h, each input is h bigger for the same output

A common misconception is to shift right because the number is positive: (x + 2)² has its bottom at x = −2, where (−2 + 2)² = 0, so the right answer slides it left and the answer (2, 0) is drawn as a slip in red; (x + 1)² − 4 slides left too, and (x + 2)³ − 1 is drawn in red as the cube slid the wrong way

Instruments convert with the linear equation y = mx + b: S(p) = 0.16p + 4 is the line 0.16p slid up by its 4 mA, so 0% sends 4 mA, 100% sends 20 mA, and the 8 mA the line gives at 50% becomes 12 mA, with the slope still 0.16 mA per percent

Every worked number is right: x² − 3 takes (1, 1) to (1, −2); √(x − 4) is 0 at 4 and has no value below it; (x − 3)² + 2 gives 2, 3 and 6 at 3, 4 and 5; (x + 1)² − 4 gives −4 at −1; (x − 2)³ − 1 gives −1 at 2 and 1 − 1 = 0 at 3; S(50) + 1 = 13 mA and S(51) = 12.16 mA
Before Check a puzzle draws no answer; the right answer slides the graph there, shows its point and draws nothing in red; each wrong answer draws its own slip in red and leaves the graph where it was

The picture tells the truth: every dot sits on its own graph at its place inside the grid, the dashed copy stays where the graph started, and a drag lands only on whole squares within the screen's limits, with the rule above rewritten to match
Every demonstration slides one whole square per hop and has settled within 4.5 s, starting after the 0.35 s screen fade; every answer, right or wrong, has arrived within 2.5 s of Check

applied.problem: "Change the input inside the bracket and it slides left or right" overreaches: after lesson 6, multiplying the input inside, f(2x), squeezes the graph instead; only adding or taking a number inside slides it.

"Outside the bracket moves it up or down" and "Inside moves it sideways" stop holding after lesson 6, where 2f(x) stretches and f(2x) squeezes; the rule is about a number added or taken away, so it is narrowed to say so.
The stated limit is false: a timer set early slides its chart left, so timers can show both directions; a real break is that a daily chart wraps round at midnight while a graph does not.
